blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Define demand as the quantity of a good that consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price over a period of time, and separate demand from a mere want and from supply.

blocks.heading: Demand, defined
blocks.text: Demand is the quantity of a good that consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price over a period of time. At the Opuwo market, buyers may take 200 bottles of Kaoko Juice in a week at N$10 a bottle: that figure, at that price, over that week, is the quantity demanded. Willingness on its own is not enough. A student who wants a bottle but has N$4 to spend wants the juice yet cannot pay, so that want stays outside demand. Demand backed by the ability to pay is called effective demand.

blocks.heading: Willing and able in practice
blocks.text: Test the definition against three buyers at the juice stall when a bottle costs N$10. Buyer A has N$12 and wants the juice: willing and able, so A demands a bottle. Buyer B has N$12 but prefers the water next door: able, yet not willing, so B adds nothing to demand. Buyer C wants the juice but has N$6: willing, yet not able, so C adds nothing either. A stall in Ho Chi Minh City in Vietnam sorts its buyers the same way: a tourist with the money but no wish adds nothing, and a student who cannot meet the day's price adds nothing either.

blocks.heading: Demand is not supply
blocks.text: The confusion learners make: demand and supply are mixed up, because both are quantities and both appear as curves in the same diagram. The boundary: demand is the buying side, the quantities buyers are willing and able to take at each price; supply, developed in topic 2.4, is the selling side, the quantities producers are willing and able to offer. The test: ask which side of the market the quantity belongs to. When demand rises, buyers take more at each price; when supply rises, sellers offer more at each price.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Every act of demand is a choice with an opportunity cost, which topic 1.3 develops; the selling side of the market follows in topic 2.4.
